title: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Larger and more dominant groups tend to keep increasing in size and to supplant smaller, feebler groups, which is why all organisms, recent and extinct, fall into a few great orders, still fewer classes, and a single natural system.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The larger and more dominant groups thus tend to go on increasing in size; and they consequently supplant many smaller and feebler groups. Thus we can account for the fact that all organisms, recent and extinct, are included under a few great orders, under still fewer classes, and all in one great natural system.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “CLASSIFICATION, groups subordinate to groups”. Scope: all higher taxa through geological time

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Parts of the proposed expansion-and-replacement mechanism are testable in well-sampled fossil groups. Explaining the entire hierarchy of life from that mechanism is underdetermined and data coverage is uneven.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define dominance by abundance, range and species richness, then use fossil time series to test whether dominant clades preferentially diversify while smaller clades decline, and whether this process predicts concentration into few high-level groups. Support requires temporal replacement rather than merely present-day imbalance.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Dominant and feeble are ambiguous and potentially circular.

Few high ranks may partly reflect classification conventions.

Fossil sampling strongly affects apparent diversity and replacement.

fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.48
data adequacy: 0.42
data existence: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.42
operationalizability: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Richness, occupancy and extinction through time are in the fossil-occurrence record, so the expansion-and-replacement half can be tested for marine animals. The further claim that this is why all life falls into a few classes is a historical explanation that the same imbalance would suggest under simpler models. A null-model analysis is feasible and would remain ambiguous about the mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Through the Phanerozoic, test whether clades that are already species-rich and widespread tend to gain further species while smaller clades decline, and whether that replacement produces the observed concentration of diversity in few higher taxa. The claim is confirmed if prior richness and occupancy predict subsequent expansion and extinction of smaller groups beyond a constant-rate null, and refuted if clade success is independent of prior dominance.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The pull of the recent and better preservation of young rocks make living groups look more dominant than they were.

Linking one group's gain to another group's extinction requires co-occurrence and interaction evidence the fossil record rarely has.

Constant-rate speciation and extinction already produce a few dominant clades, so imbalance alone does not show that large groups supplant small ones.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.55
data existence: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.45
